strengths: The paper identifies a useful MOT problem: generic ReID embeddings may benefit from adaptation to the identities present in a particular video. Applying historical trajectory labels to feature-space adaptation is simple, interpretable, and requires no additional network training.

The controlled baseline improvements are substantial. With default settings, HOTA increases from 50.6 to 58.6 on DanceTrack and from 67.3 to 78.1 on SportsMOT (Tables 1 and 3), accompanied by clear association improvements.

The evaluation spans four datasets and multiple feature extractors. Consistent gains across four MASA variants in Table 4 support applicability beyond one pretrained ReID model, although TAO improvements are smaller.

Tables 5–8 provide useful evidence for FLD versus PCA, history length, temporal weighting, and similarity fusion. Evaluating both oracle and predicted detections helps separate association improvements from detection quality.
weaknesses: The central projection is insufficiently specified for common tracking conditions. Appendix B.1 uses scipy.linalg.eigh(S_B, S_W), which requires positive-definite S_W, but high-dimensional features and short trajectory histories commonly produce singular scatter matrices. No regularization, rank reduction, or fallback is described. Handling zero or one historical identity, incomplete queues, and missing observations is also unspecified. These details are necessary to reproduce the method.

Reproducibility and tuning protocols remain incomplete. Appendix A lists tracker thresholds and EMA parameters without providing their values or search ranges; the dataset-specific settings marked † are also absent. The splits used for these searches are not clearly identified. Appendix A.3 changes MASA's matching procedure, but Table 4 does not explicitly establish whether its baseline rows use the same modified matcher.

Assessed as Algorithms/General, the methodological novelty is modest: classical FLD, exponentially weighted centroids, and similarity fusion. The related-work discussion does not adequately position this combination against online appearance adaptation and discriminative metric learning for tracking. PCA alone is a limited comparator for establishing the value of the particular adaptation mechanism.

The broad state-of-the-art claims exceed the comparison coverage. Tables 1–3 omit end-to-end trackers discussed in the manuscript and do not establish a comprehensive contemporary comparison. The simple appearance-only baseline is useful for isolation, but an experiment integrating HAT into a strong hybrid tracker would better establish its practical incremental value.

Robustness to erroneous historical identities is acknowledged but not directly tested. Because predicted assignments supervise subsequent projections, identity mistakes can reinforce themselves; aggregate improvements and qualitative feature plots do not establish when fusion prevents this failure.

Several narrower issues need correction or qualification: Eq. (6) divides the class sum by N rather than N_c; PCA maximizes retained variance rather than separating samples evenly; and the reported 22.7 FPS excludes detection and lacks baseline timing or scaling measurements. The projected 4–10× acceleration is speculative.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful MOT problem: adapting generic ReID features to distinguish identities within the current sequence. The history-conditioned Fisher projection is simple, interpretable, and requires no additional neural-network training. Under Algorithms/General, this practical contribution has value despite using established mathematics.

The reported improvements over the appearance-only baseline are substantial. With default settings, DanceTrack test HOTA increases from 50.6 to 58.6 and SportsMOT from 67.3 to 78.1. The corresponding association improvements support the central claim that the transformation improves identity discrimination.

The evaluation covers four datasets and multiple feature extractors. Table 4 reports consistent gains across four MASA variants, including modest improvements on TAO, providing evidence beyond one representation or pedestrian benchmark.

The ablations provide useful support for the design: Table 5 compares FLD against PCA with both oracle and predicted detections, while Tables 6–8 examine history length, temporal weighting, and similarity fusion. The paper also acknowledges the potential value of motion information and reports inference speed.
weaknesses: The central numerical procedure is underspecified in a consequential way. Section 3.2 requires an invertible within-class scatter matrix, and Appendix B.1 specifies scipy.linalg.eigh(S_B, S_W), which requires positive-definite S_W. With 2048-dimensional FastReID features and short trajectory histories, singular scatter matrices are unavoidable during initialization and plausible thereafter. No regularization, rank reduction, or fallback is described. The C=1 case also produces a zero-dimensional projection and undefined projected cosine similarity. These omissions prevent faithful implementation of routine tracking cases. Separately, Eq. (6) should normalize by N_c rather than N; that appears to be a correctable notation error.

The evaluation protocol is insufficiently documented. Appendix A.1 says tracker thresholds are grid-searched on the corresponding datasets but provides neither their values nor explicit tuning splits. Section 4.3 introduces dataset-specific dagger configurations without specifying the changes, whereas Appendix A.2 describes uniform transformation settings. This is not evidence of test-set tuning, but it makes the strongest results difficult to audit and reproduce. For MASA, Appendix A.3 also changes the matching procedure; Table 4 should explicitly establish that both baseline and HAT rows use the same modified matcher.

Originality is not adequately situated. The contribution combines classical FLD, exponentially weighted centroids, and similarity interpolation, but the related-work discussion does not meaningfully position it against online metric learning or adaptive appearance metrics for tracking. PCA is a useful control for dimensionality reduction, yet does not establish an advantage over alternative history-conditioned metrics. Stronger positioning and an appropriate adaptive-metric baseline would clarify the algorithmic advance.

The projection treats predicted trajectory assignments as supervision, creating a potential feedback loop in which identity errors distort later associations. Section 3.4 recognizes this risk, but the experiments do not isolate robustness to contaminated histories, identity switches, or newly appearing targets. The fusion ablation establishes an aggregate benefit without demonstrating that it addresses these specific failure modes.

The broader practical claims exceed the evidence. The method is evaluated primarily within a custom appearance-only tracker, without testing whether it improves an established hybrid tracker. Its strongest comparative result is on SportsMOT; it remains below the best listed methods on DanceTrack and MOT17. Appendix B.1 reports 22.7 FPS excluding detection, but provides no baseline throughput or runtime breakdown, leaving the accuracy–latency tradeoff unclear. These limitations do not negate the reported gains, but, together with the implementation and protocol gaps, leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful MOT problem: globally trained ReID features may inadequately distinguish similar identities within a particular sequence. Adapting the representation using historical track assignments is intuitive and practically relevant, without requiring additional network training.

The improvements over the controlled appearance-only baseline are substantial. With default settings, HOTA increases from 50.6 to 58.6 on DanceTrack and from 67.3 to 78.1 on SportsMOT. The corresponding association gains support the proposed mechanism, and the SportsMOT results exceed the compared methods.

The ablations provide meaningful evidence beyond headline results. Table 5 compares FLD with dimensionality-matched PCA under both oracle and predicted detections; Tables 6–8 investigate history length, temporal weighting, and similarity fusion. Together, these support the value of trajectory-conditioned projection.

Experiments with four MASA encoders show consistent improvements across DanceTrack, SportsMOT, and TAO, extending the evidence beyond one ReID model. The manuscript also acknowledges limitations concerning motion cues and computational cost.
weaknesses: The numerical specification of the central operation is incomplete. Equation (7) requires an invertible within-class scatter matrix, and Appendix B.1 specifies scipy.linalg.eigh(S_B, S_W), which requires positive-definite S_W. With 2048-dimensional features and short trajectory histories, S_W can be rank deficient; for standard class means its rank is at most N−C. No regularization, preliminary dimensionality reduction, or fallback is described. This is a substantive reproducibility concern because the stated solver cannot handle such cases directly.

Important online implementation details remain unspecified: initialization before sufficient history exists, handling zero or one trajectory, incomplete queues, and missing observations. Appendix A names tracker thresholds but does not provide their values or search ranges. Dataset-specific configurations marked with a dagger and their tuning splits are also insufficiently documented. These omissions prevent confident reproduction and assessment of model-selection fairness.

The originality is primarily an application of classical supervised projection, supplemented by temporal weighting and similarity fusion. This can be valuable, but the related work does not adequately position the contribution against online metric learning or adaptive appearance models. PCA alone provides limited evidence that FLD is preferable to other trajectory-conditioned metrics.

The projection learns from potentially erroneous track assignments, creating a feedback loop. Although Section 3.4 recognizes this risk, the experiments do not directly examine sensitivity to identity contamination, recovery after switches, or track births and long occlusions. Aggregate improvements establish usefulness but provide less support for the broader robustness claims.

The scope of the comparisons needs clearer qualification. The method is competitive rather than best on DanceTrack and MOT17, and its benefit within an established hybrid tracker is untested. The zero-shot claim applies to the transferred appearance models; Section 4.2 still uses target-benchmark detector weights. Appendix A.3 also changes MASA's matching procedure, so Table 4 should explicitly identify whether both baseline and HAT rows share that modification.

There are smaller presentation and efficiency issues: Equation (6) divides the class sum by N rather than N_c, Figure 4 labels the apparent PCA comparison as LDA, and the promised code link is blank. The reported 22.7 FPS excludes detection and lacks baseline timing or scaling measurements. These are secondary to the unresolved numerical and reproducibility concerns, which make the overall recommendation borderline reject despite promising empirical gains.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant MOT problem: adapting generic appearance embeddings to distinguish identities in the current sequence. Under the default Algorithms/General category, its main contribution is a practical use of history-supervised Fisher discriminant analysis, with temporal centroids and similarity fusion. The approach is conceptually simple and requires no additional backbone training.

The reported improvements are substantial. With default settings, FastReID-MOT improves from 50.6 to 58.6 HOTA on DanceTrack and from 67.3 to 78.1 on SportsMOT. Gains also transfer to hybrid trackers, including OC-SORT-ReID improving from 74.1 to 81.2 HOTA on SportsMOT. These paired comparisons provide stronger evidence than the headline state-of-the-art claims alone.

Evaluation is broad, covering multiple tracking frameworks, four MASA backbones, and five datasets including supplementary experiments. Consistent, smaller improvements on TAO support applicability beyond person tracking.

The incremental ablations are useful: Table 5 distinguishes FLD from PCA, Tables 6–8 examine history length and the two additional components, and Table 9 compares sequence-conditioned fitting with fitting on labeled training data. Holding baseline tracker parameters fixed during ablations strengthens attribution.
The manuscript acknowledges limited improvements on MOT17, reports computational overhead, and discusses unsuccessful variants. These disclosures help establish the method’s practical scope.
weaknesses: The central numerical procedure is insufficiently specified. Appendix B.5 states that scipy.linalg.eigh(S_B, S_W) is used, which requires positive-definite S_W. Under Eq. (3), rank(S_W) is at most N−C, so the matrix is necessarily singular when the available history contains too few samples relative to the reported 2048-dimensional features, particularly during startup. No regularization, rank reduction, or fallback is described. Handling zero or one existing trajectory is also unspecified. These choices are essential to reproducing the algorithm and may materially affect its learned metric.

The projection objective and temporal modification need greater precision. Equation (6) presents a matrix quotient without defining a scalar optimization criterion. Section 4.2 specifies temporally weighted centroids for the between-class scatter but leaves unclear whether the within-class scatter uses the same centers or weights. Because the final association uses cosine similarity, the eigenvector normalization and exact projection convention also matter. These ambiguities go beyond a cosmetic notation correction.

Experimental reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive tables. Appendix A.2 lists baseline hyperparameters but omits their selected values and search ranges; the validation protocol for dataset-specific tuning is not consistently explicit. Exact checkpoint choices and hybrid integration rules are also insufficiently detailed. Appendix A.3 changes MASA’s matching procedure and tunes its parameters, so Table 3 should clearly identify the reproduced baseline configuration and distinguish the effect of these changes from HAT.

The evidence supports a useful adaptation mechanism more strongly than the broad novelty and conceptual claims. FLD, temporal weighting, and score fusion are established techniques, while the related-work discussion does not adequately position the contribution against online discriminative appearance learning and metric adaptation. PCA and globally fitted FLD are informative controls, but comparisons with simpler sequence-conditioned centering or whitening would help establish why trajectory-supervised FLD is needed. Describing generic ReID matching as fundamentally inappropriate is also stronger than the results warrant.

Robustness and efficiency claims need qualification. Aggregate benchmarks do not isolate feedback from incorrect historical assignments or performance on newly arriving identities, although these motivate similarity fusion. Runtime falls from 46.5 to 22.7 FPS even before detector latency, and scaling with track count is not measured. The projected 4–10× acceleration is speculative. Together with the unresolved solver and protocol details, these concerns narrowly outweigh the strong empirical gains in the current submission.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful MOT problem: adapting generic ReID features to the identities present in the current sequence. Applying FLD using historical track assignments is conceptually simple, requires no additional network training, and can complement existing trackers.

The reported improvements are substantial. With default settings, FastReID-MOT improves from 50.6 to 58.6 HOTA on DanceTrack and from 67.3 to 78.1 on SportsMOT. Improvements also extend to hybrid trackers, including OC-SORT-ReID increasing from 74.1 to 81.2 HOTA on SportsMOT.

Evaluation has meaningful breadth: multiple tracking frameworks, four MASA backbones, and DanceTrack, SportsMOT, TAO, MOT17, and MOT20. The consistent MASA improvements support applicability beyond one feature extractor.

The ablations compare FLD against PCA and globally fitted supervised FLD, and examine history length, temporal weighting, and similarity fusion. These experiments support the practical value of sequence-specific adaptation. The appendix also candidly discusses runtime and weaker gains on MOT17.
weaknesses: The central numerical procedure is insufficiently specified. Appendix B.5 states that the implementation uses scipy.linalg.eigh(S_B, S_W), which requires a positive-definite second matrix. However, the within-class scatter has rank at most N−C under the standard centroids and will be singular when short track histories provide fewer samples than the 2048 feature dimensions; initialization is especially problematic. No regularization, rank reduction, or fallback is described. Handling fewer than two tracks is also unspecified. These are consequential reproducibility gaps in the core algorithm, rather than merely presentation issues.

The projection's mathematical definition needs clarification. Equation (6) divides matrices without defining a scalar objective or normalization constraint. Section 4.2 explicitly discusses inserting weighted centroids into the between-class scatter, but does not clearly specify whether the within-class scatter changes as well. These choices affect the resulting projection and cosine similarities.

Experimental reproducibility is incomplete. Appendix A.2 lists baseline hyperparameters but omits their selected values and search ranges. The splits used for dataset-specific tuning, particularly the dagger-marked results, are not clearly identified. MASA's matching procedure is modified, and the custom ByteTrack-ReID and OC-SORT-ReID integrations lack sufficient implementation detail. This does not establish leakage or unfairness, but makes the comparisons difficult to independently verify.

The novelty and conceptual claims are broader than the evidence establishes. The method combines classical FLD, temporal centroid weighting, and score fusion. PCA and globally fitted FLD are useful controls, but do not distinguish its advantages from other simple online metric adaptations. The conclusion that conventional ReID matching is fundamentally inappropriate is stronger than demonstrating that adaptation improves it; the successful fusion explicitly retains the original representation.

The proposed explanation for robustness remains only indirectly tested. Tracking errors supply the supervision for subsequent projections, creating potential error reinforcement, while new identities are absent from the fitted classes. Aggregate improvements and the fusion ablation are encouraging, but targeted experiments on corrupted histories, identity switches, and object arrivals would better substantiate the claimed remedy.

Practical benefits have a substantial computational cost: throughput falls from 46.5 to 22.7 FPS on DanceTrack, excluding detection. No comparable scaling measurements are supplied for crowded scenes. Together with the unresolved numerical and reproducibility details, this leaves a slight preference for rejection despite the strong reported accuracy gains.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful MOT problem: generic ReID features may be suboptimal for distinguishing the particular identities within a video. Using historical track assignments to fit a sequence-specific FLD projection is a simple, interpretable contribution with practical value.

The improvements are substantial and extend beyond the authors' appearance-only baseline. With default settings, HAT improves FastReID-MOT HOTA from 50.6 to 58.6 on DanceTrack and from 67.3 to 78.1 on SportsMOT. OC-SORT-ReID also improves from 60.8 to 64.6 and from 74.1 to 81.2, respectively.

Evaluation covers multiple tracking settings and feature extractors. The consistent improvements across four MASA backbones, including TAO, strengthen the evidence that the approach is not specific to one ReID model. The smaller gains on MOT17 appropriately reveal limits to its usefulness.

The ablations provide meaningful support for the design: comparisons with PCA and globally supervised FLD test the importance of trajectory-conditioned projection, while incremental experiments isolate temporal weighting and similarity fusion. The appendix also reports runtime and discusses limitations candidly.
weaknesses: The numerical implementation of the central FLD step is materially underspecified. Appendix B.5 uses scipy.linalg.eigh(S_B, S_W), which requires positive-definite S_W, but ordinary within-class scatter has rank at most N-C and is necessarily singular when history is insufficient for the 2048-dimensional features. This is particularly relevant during initialization and short histories. The paper does not specify regularization, rank reduction, or fallback behavior for fewer than two tracks. These choices affect both reproducibility and the resulting cosine similarities. Equation (6) also needs a precise multidimensional objective rather than a matrix quotient.

The tuning protocol is not sufficiently reproducible. Sections 5.2 and A.2 describe exhaustive dataset-specific grid searches but do not provide the selected baseline parameters, search ranges, or clearly identify the data splits used for every tuning decision, including the dagger-marked results. The transferred default configuration is useful evidence, but the strongest tuned comparisons require clearer separation of validation and test evaluation. Hybrid-tracker integration details are also sparse.

Algorithmic originality is moderate: the method combines classical FLD, temporal weighting, and similarity interpolation. The empirical application is valuable, but the claim that sequence-specific optimization has been absent from previous methodologies needs stronger positioning against online appearance adaptation and metric learning. Likewise, saying direct ReID matching is 'fundamentally inappropriate' goes beyond demonstrating that adaptation often improves it. The DanceTrack claim of surpassing SambaMOTR conflicts with Table 1, where 66.9 HOTA is below 67.2.

Robustness to erroneous historical labels is asserted more than directly evaluated. Aggregate gains and the fusion ablation are encouraging, but there is no targeted analysis of error propagation, identity switches, newborn objects, or abrupt appearance changes. These are important because the method learns its next association metric from its own previous assignments.

The practical cost is considerable: throughput falls from 46.5 to 22.7 FPS on DanceTrack, excluding detection. Runtime and memory scaling with crowd density, history length, and feature dimension are not measured. The suggested 4–10× acceleration is explicitly an estimate and should not support efficiency claims.
